Four explanations have circulated in the valley: fertilizer washing off the upper fields; warm water leaving the mill's outflow; a timber jam that slows the current at the narrows; and the loss of the mussels that once filtered the shallows. Reyes spent five summers deciding among them.

The evidence is for the jam: the logs piled up in 1977, and the water behind them stands still. The inflow tests no richer in phosphate than the springs, though fertilizer is spread up there still. The mill's water leaves no warmer than the lake, and the green is thickest a mile above it. The mussel beds still hold the shallows in numbers, and the divers find living shell.

Reyes draws the shoreline herself, sitting on the gravel with a board to sketch each bay. Nobody stops at the mouth to extract water by hand, since a fixed gauge takes the samples. The morning count does not attract a crowd, and nobody comes down to the gravel to watch. No boat is dragged up the gravel here, since the crew wade out from the shingle.

What the mill's ledger supplies is a price: the clerk entered what the mill charged for grinding. No date is entered in the ledger, whose years the clerk left blank. No count of sacks appears in the ledger, whose columns were never totalled. No name is written in the ledger, the lease being held by the parish.

The cure follows the cause: pulling the timber jam from the narrows would clear the water. Keeping the fertilizer off the fields was tried in 1991, and the August green came anyway. Cooling the water that leaves the mill was tried in 1994, and the green came anyway. Putting mussels back in the shallows was tried in 1999, and the green came anyway. The method is open to doubt, for five summers of jars decide nothing. I will not say flatly that the case is proved, for a further summer is wanted. Nor will I call the case likely, since likely claims more than the jars carry. The finding is of no small consequence, for the green closes the shore to swimmers.

Kestrel Falls ran three bus routes to an emptying town; after 2011 ridership climbed by half. Four explanations are offered around the council table: the fare cut to a dollar; the new route out to the county hospital; the parking charge brought in downtown; and the move of the high school to the north end. Ochoa's office weighed the four.

The counts are for the school move: half the new trips are made by students going north. The dollar fare began four years before the climb, and riding fell in each of those years. The hospital route was cut to one morning trip in 2009 and has carried almost nobody since. The parking charge downtown was voted down twice and has never been collected.

The service stops at a line that marks the county boundary on the map. No route in the town is called a line, and the office knows its three routes by number. No line of people stands waiting at the depot door, since riders scatter along the kerb. No line of printed words appears at the foot of the timetable, which carries figures only.

What the driver's log supplies is a weather note: each driver marks rain, ice or clear. No count of riders is marked in the log, and the depot adds no totals from it. No time of leaving is marked in the log, and no sheet of minutes is filed. No name is signed in the log, the depot assigning its buses by ticket instead.

The finding runs the other way too: moving the high school back would drop the riders away. Raising the fare above a dollar was tried in 2016, and nobody stopped riding. Closing the hospital route was tried in the winter of 2017, and nobody stopped riding. Lifting the parking charge was tried in 2018, and nobody stopped riding. The finding is proved and of small consequence: the town empties either way. I will not say flatly that the finding is proved, for another year of counts is wanted. Nor will I call the finding likely, since likely claims more than the counts carry. I doubt neither the method nor the counting behind it.
